profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a climate data lab that is rebuilding NOAA AVHRR-based Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) products for a public archive of U.S. drought history. The immediate problem is that the reprocessed maps for the 1988 drought show weaker stress in the central Plains and a later onset than the examples reported from the original 1985-90 NOAA work. The agenda is to compare what each person thinks the current pipeline is doing, identify the most plausible reason for the mismatch, and agree on the next diagnostic rerun before the archive release. The expected outcome is a concrete troubleshooting plan for one revised processing run that should bring the regenerated VCI sequence closer to the historical late-1980s drought record.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: AVHRR vegetation indices, drought interpretation, historical satellite-climate comparisons
members.background: Lena previously worked on retrospective drought monitoring projects and has spent several years comparing satellite-derived vegetation stress maps with precipitation and crop-yield anomalies from the 1980s.
members.private_state: She wants the rebuilt product to be scientifically comparable to the historical NOAA examples and worries that quiet modernization choices are changing the meaning of the index while still looking technically clean.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the pipeline is using the weekly composite, they mean the original NOAA operational 7-day compositing windows used in the late-1980s product, not generic calendar weeks.
The VCI baseline should be derived from the 1985-1990 study-era record and be week-specific, because that is the frame used in the published late-1980s drought examples she is trying to reproduce.

If the result matches the paper, that means the onset week and local severity pattern over the central Plains and western Corn Belt align closely enough to support scientific comparison, not just that the general summer footprint looks similar.
Current archive documentation is implementation-oriented and does not automatically override assumptions from the original scientific methodology.

members.name: Evan Brooks
members.expertise: Earth observation pipelines, satellite archive harmonization, reproducible geospatial processing
members.background: Evan leads the modernization of legacy environmental datasets into cloud-based workflows and is used to replacing undocumented historical conventions with standardized processing choices when metadata appear equivalent.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the rebuild reproducible and maintainable in the modern archive, and he is trying to avoid adding special-case logic that only exists to mimic historical quirks.
hidden_assumptions: When people say weekly composite, they mean a standard Monday-Sunday aggregation aligned with the current archive scheduler, because that is the most reproducible interpretation of weekly products.

The baseline or climatology for VCI should use the full stable reprocessed archive span available for that build, which in practice means extending beyond 1985-1990 when consistent data already exist.
If the result lines up with the paper, that means the regional drought pattern over summer resembles the published maps at a broad scale, even if exact onset timing shifts by a composite or two.
Archive-side standardization decisions are already part of the accepted processing context unless a paper explicitly forbids them.

misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'match the paper' sounds precise because both know the same publication, but each silently applies a different standard of fidelity appropriate to their own work.
